message.content:
Below is a concise but thorough overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (All information is current as of October 2026; laws can change, so check the Texas Property Code or consult an attorney if you need up‑to‑date advice.) | # | Right / Protection | What it Means | Practical Tips | |---|--------------------|---------------|----------------| | **1** | **Security Deposit Limits** | Landlords may charge a maximum of **one month’s rent** for a single‑unit dwelling and **two months’ rent** for a multi‑unit building. | Keep a copy of the lease and any receipt for the deposit. | | **2** | **Deposit Return** | Landlord must return the deposit (minus lawful deductions) within **30 days** after you move out, unless you agree to a longer period in writing. | Request a written itemized list of deductions. | | **3** | **Habitability** | Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition—plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc. | Document any problems with photos and written notices. | | **4** | **Repair & Deduct** | If the landlord fails to fix a major issue within a reasonable time, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent (or pay the landlord and then recover). | Keep receipts and give the landlord written notice before acting. | | **5** | **Notice Requirements** | • **Rent Increase**: 30‑day notice for increases < 25% of current rent. 60‑day notice for increases ≥ 25%.
• **Lease Termination**: 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month leases; 60‑day notice for longer leases. | Use certified mail or a delivery service that provides proof of receipt. | | **6** | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | Landlord cannot enter without proper notice (usually 24‑hour written notice) except in emergencies. | Keep a log of any unannounced entries. | | **7** | **Anti‑Discrimination** | Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes (Fair Housing Act). | Report violations to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **8** | **Eviction Process** | Landlord must follow the Texas Property Code: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 30‑day notice for lease violation), file an unlawful detainer action, and obtain a court judgment. | Do not leave the property until the court orders you to do so. | | **9** | **Right to a Written Lease** | While not required, having a written lease protects both parties. | Ask for a copy of the lease and read it carefully before signing. | | **10** | **Right to Disclose Health Hazards** | Landlord must disclose known health hazards (e.g., lead paint, mold). | Request a lead hazard disclosure form if the building was built before 1978. | | **11** | **Right to Privacy** | Landlord must respect your privacy; they can’t conduct searches without a warrant or court order. | Keep a record of any suspicious activity. | | **12** | **Right to Fair Rent** | Landlord cannot charge more than the market rate for comparable units in the same area. | Research local listings to confirm fairness. | | **13** | **Right to a Safe Environment** | Landlord must maintain fire safety equipment, smoke detectors, and secure locks. | Test smoke detectors monthly and report failures. | | **14** | **Right to a Written Notice of Eviction** | Landlord must provide a written notice before filing an eviction lawsuit. | Verify that the notice is in compliance with Texas law. | | **15** | **Right to File a Complaint** | You can file complaints with HUD, the Texas Commission on Human Rights, or the local housing authority. | Gather documentation (photos, receipts, correspondence). | ### Quick Reference Checklist 1. **Ask for a written lease** – read it thoroughly. 2. **Document everything** – photos, videos, written notices, receipts. 3. **Know the notice periods** – 30 days for rent increase < 25%, 60 days for ≥ 25%; 30 days for month‑to‑month termination. 4. **Keep a copy of the security deposit receipt** – and know the 30‑day return rule. 5. **Report repairs promptly** – give written notice, keep records. 6. **Know your eviction timeline** – 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 30‑day notice for lease violations. 7. **Use certified mail** for all written communications. ### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Property Code** | Statutory tenant‑landlord law | https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/ | | **HUD – Fair Housing** | Complaint filing, education | https://www.hud.gov/ | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Discrimination complaints | https://www.tchra.org/ | | **Local Housing Authority** | Eviction mediation, legal aid | Search your city’s official website | | **Legal Aid of North Texas** | Free legal assistance | https://www.lanxtx.org/ | | **Texas Tenant Hotline** | Quick answers to common questions | 1‑800‑555‑1234 (example) | --- #### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you’re entitled to a safe, habitable home, fair treatment, and clear communication from your landlord. Keep records, understand the notice requirements, and use the resources above if you encounter problems. If you’re facing a serious dispute (e.g., eviction, discrimination, major repairs), consider consulting a qualified attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
